R05-A-01: Imagine a cinema that sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub at a modest price and a large tub at nearly twice that. Most customers buy the small one, until the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub priced only slightly below the large. Hardly anyone buys the medium, yet sales of the large tub rise sharply, so that the new option has done its work without ever being chosen. It exists to make the large tub look like a bargain, and in many such cases it succeeds; marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it produces turns up often enough, with magazine subscriptions, holiday packages and software plans as well as snacks, to deserve a more careful explanation than the claim that customers are easily fooled. The standard account of choice in economics assumes that a person arrives at a shop with a ranking of the available goods already settled, and that the shop merely reveals it. On that account the decoy should be inert: if I prefer the small tub to the large one, the arrival of a medium tub that I do not want should leave my ranking of the other two untouched. What the decoy suggests instead is that many preferences are not retrieved but assembled on the spot, from the comparisons the menu makes easy. The medium tub is easy to compare with the large, being the same product at almost the same price with visibly less popcorn, whereas the comparison between the small and the large, which requires trading money against quantity, is considerably harder. Consequently, people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one. It would be a mistake to conclude that preferences are endlessly pliable, for the effect is strongest when buyers are unsure what they want and have little experience of the product; a regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat is rarely moved. It also weakens when the decoy is so plainly inferior that customers notice the trick, and resentment at being steered can push them the other way. These limits matter, because they show that the decoy exploits a gap in knowledge rather than a defect of reason: constructing a preference out of whatever comparisons are available is a perfectly sensible strategy for someone who lacks better information. The more interesting lesson concerns the menu itself. We usually treat the set of options as neutral background and the decision as the thing to be explained, but the decoy shows that the background is part of the decision. Whoever arranges the options, whether a cinema, a software firm setting its subscription tiers or a restaurant pricing its wine list, is not merely displaying choices but helping to form them. This does not make every arrangement sinister, since some arrangement is unavoidable, but it does mean that the question of what people chose cannot be separated from the question of what they were shown.
R05-A-02: Suppose a dozen firms bid for the right to drill in a tract of seabed whose reserves nobody knows, and that each firm commissions its own survey, and the surveys, being estimates, scatter around the true figure, some too high and some too low. If each firm bids what its own survey says the tract is worth, the contract will go to the firm whose survey was most optimistic, so that winning, in other words, is itself evidence of having overestimated. The firm that celebrates its victory has been selected for its error, and it will on average pay more than the tract is worth. This phenomenon is the winner's curse, and the striking thing about it is that no bidder needs to be foolish for it to occur, since each estimate may be honest and, taken alone, unbiased. The remedy, in principle, is simple: a bidder should ask not what the tract is worth given its survey, but what it is worth given its survey and given that it has won. The second question yields a lower number, and a bidder who answers it will shade its bid below the raw estimate, more sharply the more rivals there are, since the highest of many estimates is more likely to be inflated than the highest of a few. Shading of this kind is not timidity but the correct response to a feature of the situation that the unconditioned estimate ignores. A natural objection is that the curse should vanish with experience, because firms that overpay will lose money, notice and adjust, while those that do not will be driven from the market. There is truth in this, and seasoned bidders in many settings do shade their bids, but the learning is slower than the objection supposes. The outcome of any single auction is noisy, since a tract that disappoints may simply have been unlucky. Worse, the firms that lose never discover what the prize was really worth, so the information that would correct everyone's estimates is gathered only by the winners, and slowly. A lesson that must be extracted from a few expensive and ambiguous victories is not quickly learned. For this reason the design of an auction matters as much as the wisdom of its participants. Formats in which bids are revealed as they rise allow each bidder to watch rivals drop out and to infer something about their estimates, and a bidder who can see how far others are willing to go has less reason to fear that its own enthusiasm is an error. Sealed bids, by contrast, leave each participant alone with a single survey and its uncorrected optimism. The point is not that one format is always superior, since open bidding has weaknesses of its own, among them the ease with which rivals can signal to one another, but that the curse is a property of the information structure, and so can be eased by changing that structure rather than by exhorting bidders to be cleverer.
R05-A-03: A great deal of advertising tells the viewer almost nothing. A television spot in which a famous athlete drinks a soft drink on a beach conveys no fact about the drink's price, ingredients or taste that a sceptical viewer could check, and critics of advertising have long drawn what seems the obvious conclusion: if the message carries no information, the money spent on it is either wasted or devoted to manipulation, persuading people to want things by associating them with glamour. The conclusion is natural, but it rests on the assumption that whatever an advertisement communicates must be contained in what it says or shows, and that assumption is open to question. Consider the matter from the firm's side. A company launching a product that is cheap to try, such as a breakfast cereal or a shampoo, makes its money not from the first purchase but from the repeat purchases of customers who liked it. A firm confident that its product is good therefore expects a long stream of returns from anyone it persuades to try it once, whereas a firm that knows its product is mediocre expects most of those who try it never to return. Lavish advertising is accordingly worth far more to the first firm than to the second, and a consumer who sees a product advertised extravagantly may reasonably infer that its maker is wagering on repeat business. On this view the expense of the advertisement is itself the message, and the athlete and the beach matter chiefly because everyone can see that they cost a fortune. The argument has real force, but its reach is limited. It applies most clearly to what economists call experience goods, whose quality can be judged only after use, and only where repeat purchase is likely; a firm selling something that people buy once in a lifetime gains little from the signal, because satisfied customers will not return in any case. For goods whose qualities can be inspected before purchase, such as the dimensions of a table or the fare for a train journey, advertising informs directly and requires no signalling story at all. Nor does the argument show that every extravagant campaign is a reliable signal, since a firm may overspend from vanity or miscalculation, and imitators may learn to mimic the outward appearance of expense more cheaply than it seems. A familiar objection is that ordinary consumers do not reason in this way, since nobody watching a soft drink advertisement contemplates the economics of repeat purchase. The objection misunderstands what the argument requires. Consumers need not reconstruct the logic; it is enough that they follow a rule of thumb, such as trusting brands they have heard of, and that the rule tends, on the whole, to reward them. The signalling account does not vindicate advertising, and it leaves the question of manipulation entirely open. What it does establish is that an advertisement without content is not, for that reason alone, an advertisement without meaning.
R05-A-04: Defenders of nudging, the practice of steering choices by altering how options are presented rather than by forbidding or taxing any of them, have a ready answer to the charge that it is manipulative. Someone, they point out, must decide which option on a form is pre-selected, which dish stands at eye level in a canteen and which paragraph of a letter comes first; since there is no presentation without some arrangement, the choice is not between influencing people and leaving them alone but between influencing them thoughtfully and influencing them carelessly. The argument is sound as far as it goes, and critics who speak as though an unarranged menu were available are attacking a position nobody holds. Yet the argument from inevitability answers a weaker objection than the one that matters. What troubles the more careful critics is not that choice architects influence us, which is unavoidable, but that many of the most effective nudges work precisely to the extent that they go unnoticed. A default enrolment in a savings scheme succeeds partly because inertia keeps people where they were placed, but also because many never register that a decision was made on their behalf; a smaller plate reduces consumption chiefly when diners do not reflect that they have been served less. Influence of this sort does not engage the faculties by which people govern themselves, but routes around them. One way to sharpen the worry is to ask whether a given nudge would survive disclosure. Suppose a canteen posted a notice explaining that fruit had been placed at the front because the management wanted employees to eat more of it. If the arrangement continues to work, its power did not depend on concealment, and it begins to look less like manipulation than like a reminder. If it stops working once explained, that is evidence that it relied on a gap between what people were doing and what they understood themselves to be doing, and an institution that relies on such gaps owes its public a justification that it cannot easily give in public. The test is not decisive in every case, and it should not be mistaken for a general condemnation. Some nudges would plainly survive disclosure: a letter telling people that most of their neighbours pay their taxes on time would plausibly work whether or not recipients knew why it had been sent, since the information is itself the influence. Others might fail it for innocent reasons, because a disclosure can itself distract, or can provoke a reflexive contrariness that has nothing to do with the merits of the option. What the test accomplishes is to shift the debate from an unanswerable question, whether influence is present, to an answerable one, whether the influence could be avowed. That shift concedes to the defenders everything their best argument actually establishes, and withholds from them only what it never established.
R05-A-05: When information was scarce, the economic problem it posed was one of supply: how to print, carry and store enough of it for the people who wanted it. That problem has largely been solved, and its solution has exposed another. The abundance of material has made scarce the one resource that every piece of it requires, namely the attention of those who are meant to receive it. Every article, message and video competes for the same limited hours of the same limited minds, and while the cost of producing one more piece of content has fallen almost to nothing, the supply of attention has not grown at all. This shift explains a feature of modern commerce that once seemed puzzling, the enormous number of services offered at no charge. A search engine, a social network or a mobile game that costs its user nothing is not a gift; it is paid for with attention, which the provider gathers and resells to advertisers, so that the user is less a customer than a supplier of the commodity being traded. Described in this way, the arrangement is not obviously unfair. Many people would gladly exchange a few seconds of distraction for a useful map or a convenient way of keeping in touch with distant friends, and for them the bargain may be a good one. The difficulty lies elsewhere, in the fact that the price is never stated. When a product is sold for money, its price is a number that buyers can compare across sellers, and the comparison disciplines firms, since a shop that charges too much loses its customers to a cheaper rival. Attention has no such number attached to it. A user cannot easily tell whether one free application takes ten minutes of her day or two hours, still less whether a rival would take less, and so the competitive pressure that keeps money prices in check operates feebly, if at all. Firms competing for attention are therefore rewarded not for charging less of it but for extracting more, and the design of their products follows accordingly, towards endless feeds, automatic playback and notifications timed to recapture a wandering mind. It does not follow that free services should be prohibited or that their users are dupes. What follows is narrower and, in a way, more practical: a market in which one side cannot see the price it pays will not protect that side as markets ordinarily do, and remedies should therefore aim at making the price visible. A service that reported to each user, plainly and regularly, how much time it had absorbed would not end the trade in attention, but it would give its users what every functioning market requires, a figure to compare.
R05-A-06: In most markets the price does the work of allocation. If more people want a good than there are units of it, the price rises until the excess disappears, and whoever is willing to pay the new price obtains the good. But there is a family of markets in which this mechanism cannot operate, because each side must choose the other. A university cannot simply admit whoever is willing to pay the most, nor can an applicant simply buy a place; a hospital hiring junior doctors cares which doctors it gets, and the doctors care which hospital they join. In such markets, sometimes called matching markets, a transaction requires mutual acceptance, and no single number can bring about a match that both sides want. Left to themselves, matching markets tend to fail in characteristic ways. One is unravelling: because the strongest candidates are in demand, employers try to secure them by making offers earlier than their rivals, and the competition for earliness can push offers so far forward that they are made before anyone knows how good the candidates are. Another is congestion: when offers must be accepted or refused quickly, a candidate holding one offer may not learn in time of a better one, and the market clears without having considered all its possibilities. A third is strategic misrepresentation, in which participants conceal their true preferences, ranking a likely option first rather than the one they actually want, because they fear that revealing their real wishes will cost them. The remedy that has often been adopted is not deregulation but construction: a clearinghouse to which both sides submit ranked lists, and which computes an assignment by a procedure known to have certain properties. The property most often sought is stability, meaning that there is no applicant and employer, not matched to each other, who would both prefer to be. A stable assignment removes the motive to break ranks, since no such pair can do better by striking a private deal, and with a suitable procedure at least one side can be given no reason to misreport its preferences. Such clearinghouses show that a market is not always a spontaneous order arising wherever people are free to trade; it can be an artefact, built to solve problems that freedom alone creates. None of this means that design can substitute for the willingness of participants. A clearinghouse works only if enough of both sides join it, and an elegant procedure is useless if the most sought-after employers find it more profitable to recruit privately. Nor can a procedure deliver every desirable property at once: no procedure, for instance, can give both sides complete reason to report honestly while always producing stable outcomes. The designer chooses among imperfect options, and the choice reflects judgements about whose interests deserve protection. The engineering of markets is thus a political as well as a technical art, but it is an art that can be practised well or badly, and the difference matters to the people whose lives it arranges.
R05-A-07: For a long time economists were embarrassed by a simple question. Water is essential to life and diamonds are not, yet water is cheap and diamonds are dear; how could prices, which were supposed to reflect value, so plainly invert the order of importance? Eighteenth-century writers posed the puzzle as a contrast between value in use and value in exchange, and many concluded that exchange value must therefore have some source other than usefulness. The most influential answer located that source in the costs of production, and above all in labour: diamonds are dear because finding and cutting them takes enormous effort, while water, in most places, merely has to be collected. The cost theory had obvious merits, since goods that are hard to produce are frequently expensive, but it struggled with cases in which effort and price come apart. A pearl found by chance in an oyster served at dinner fetches no less than one obtained by days of diving, and a wine from a celebrated year commands its price long after the labour that made it has been forgotten. The resolution that eventually prevailed, worked out independently by several writers in the later nineteenth century, abandoned the attempt to attach value to goods as such. What matters, it held, is not the usefulness of water in general but the usefulness of one more unit of it to someone who already has a certain amount. A person with enough water to drink, cook and wash would gain little from an extra bucket, while a person with few diamonds, or none, would prize one more highly. Price tracks this marginal usefulness, not the total. The resolution is genuine, and its elegance is rightly admired. But it achieved both more than it is usually credited with and less. It achieved more because it moved value from things to situations: the same bucket of water is nearly worthless in a town beside a river and beyond price to a traveller lost in a desert, although nothing about the water has changed. It achieved less because it was never a theory of importance. To say that water is cheap is to say that, where it is plentiful, nobody would give much for one more unit of it; it is not to say that water matters little. The marginal account explains why prices may be low on goods that are indispensable, and in doing so it warns us against reading prices as a ranking of what matters. That warning is regularly forgotten. Public argument often treats the market price of something as the measure of its contribution, so that an activity commanding high prices is assumed to be more valuable to society than one commanding low ones, and resources that cost nothing, such as clean air, are treated as though they were of no account until they become scarce. The marginal theory does not license this inference; if anything it predicts the error, since it shows that abundance alone can drive a price towards zero whatever the total importance of the good. Abundance, moreover, is not always permanent, and a price set while a resource was plentiful says little about what it will be worth once it is not. None of this is a case against prices, which remain an unrivalled means of coordinating what millions of people do with information that no single mind possesses. It is a case for remembering what question a price answers. A price tells us what one more unit of something is worth to those at the margin, here and now. It does not tell us what the whole of it is worth, or what it would be worth to people who are not in the market at all, and a society that forgets the difference may discover the value of its cheapest goods only when it is too late to pay for them.
R05-A-08: Give a group of people an ordinary object, a coffee mug, say, or a pen, and then ask them how much they would accept to sell it; ask another group, who were not given the object, how much they would pay to acquire one. In experiments of this kind the sellers' prices have repeatedly been found to exceed the buyers' by a wide margin, even though the two groups were formed at random and there is no reason to think that the owners care more for mugs. Merely owning a thing, it seems, makes it more valuable to its owner. The finding has come to be known as the endowment effect, and it has become one of the best-known results in behavioural economics. The standard interpretation explains it by loss aversion. People, on this view, evaluate outcomes not in absolute terms but as gains and losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Once the mug is mine, giving it up registers as a loss, whereas acquiring it, for someone who does not own it, registers only as a gain, and since the loss weighs more heavily, the owner demands more in compensation than the non-owner will pay. The account is economical, and it connects the mug experiments with a wide range of other behaviour, from the reluctance of investors to sell shares that have fallen in value to the stubbornness with which people defend entitlements they have only recently acquired. A rival interpretation treats the gap as, at least in part, an artefact of the way such experiments are conducted. Participants who have never sold anything in a laboratory may be unsure what is being asked, may suspect that the experimenter knows the object's true value, or may simply apply a rule from everyday life, never to sell for less than it would cost to replace the thing. When procedures are altered so that participants practise the bidding mechanism and understand that misstating their values cannot help them, some studies have found the gap to shrink considerably. Supporters of this view also point out that professional traders, who buy and sell as a matter of routine, appear to show much less of the effect in the goods they deal in. Each interpretation captures something real, and the dispute is less sharp than it is sometimes made to appear. The traders' case is telling not because it refutes loss aversion but because it suggests where loss aversion applies. A dealer who holds a stock of mugs holds them in order to sell them; parting with one is the purpose of having it, and so it does not register as a loss. A person who has been given a mug to use is in a different position, because the mug has already become, in a small way, part of her possessions, and parting with it means giving something up rather than completing a transaction. On this reading, what matters is not ownership as such but the frame in which a thing is held, as something to use or as something to exchange. That reading has consequences beyond the laboratory. It implies that the gap between buying and selling prices is not a fixed constant of human nature, to be entered into economic models as a permanent correction, but a variable that depends on how people come to think of what they have. Markets that encourage people to regard their possessions as stock, as resale platforms arguably do, may weaken the effect; arrangements that encourage people to regard what they hold as their own, as long trial periods for products arguably do, may strengthen it. Whether either tendency is desirable is a separate question. The point is that the endowment effect, properly understood, is less a fact about objects or owners than a fact about the relation between them.
